[[Life expectancy at birth]] in Nigeria increased from 49.4 years in 2007 to approximately 54 years in 2017.<ref name="LE">{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN?locations=NG|title=Life expectancy at birth, total (years)|website=data.worldbank.org|access-date=22 September 2019}}</ref> The under-five mortality rate (U5MR) per 1,000 live births decreased from 145.7 in 2007 to 100.2 in 2017.<ref name="data.worldbank.org">{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.DYN.MORT|title=Mortality rate, under-5 (per 1,000 live births)|website=data.worldbank.org|access-date=19 September 2019}}</ref> When compared with other countries and global averages, Nigeria's health indicators remain poor.

Sanitation infrastructure remains inadequate. Most households rely on septic tanks as centralized sewage systems are limited to [[Abuja]] and parts of [[Lagos]].<ref name="USAID">USAID: [https://web.archive.org/web/20090730015346/http://pdf.usaid.gov/pdf_docs/PNADO937.pdf Nigeria Water and Sanitation Profile], ca. 2007</ref> A 2006 study revealed that only 1% of Lagos households were connected to sewer systems.<ref>Matthew Gandy:[http://hdr.undp.org/en/reports/global/hdr2006/papers/Gandy%20Matthew.pdf Water, Sanitation, and the Modern City: Colonial and post-colonial experiences in Lagos and Mumbai], Human Development Report Office Occasional Paper, 2006</ref> In 2016, unsafe water, poor sanitation, and hygiene accounted for 68.6 deaths per 100,000 people.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.STA.WASH.P5?locations=NG|title=Mortality rate attributed to unsafe water, unsafe sanitation and lack of hygiene (per 100,000 population)|access-date=2019-09-21}}</ref>
